description: A fifth Level 1 - Math I (Physics) exam set covering differentiation, limits, integration, complex numbers, series, vector spaces, linear systems, and diagonalisation.
instructions: All main questions carry the same number of marks.
Show sufficient working to justify each answer.
Begin each main question on a new page.
label: Paper 1

questions.stem: This question concerns product rules, algebraic limits, implicit differentiation, and first-principles differentiation.
questions.title: Derivatives and limiting behaviour

parts.answer: Use the product rule with \(u=e^{2x}\) and \(v=\cos x\). Then \(u'=2e^{2x}\) and \(v'=-\sin x\), so \(h'(x)=2e^{2x}\cos x-e^{2x}\sin x=e^{2x}(2\cos x-\sin x)\). At \(x=0\), \(h'(0)=1(2-0)=2\).
parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Differentiate \(h(x)=e^{2x}\cos x\), and evaluate \(h'(0)\).

parts.answer: Direct substitution gives \(0/0\), so rationalise the numerator: \(\frac{\sqrt{1+5x}-1}{x}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{1+5x}+1}{\sqrt{1+5x}+1}=\frac{5x}{x(\sqrt{1+5x}+1)}\). For \(x\ne0\), this is \(\frac{5}{\sqrt{1+5x}+1}\). Taking \(x\to0\) gives \(5/(1+1)=5/2\).
parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Evaluate \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sqrt{1+5x}-1}{x}\).

parts.answer: Differentiate \(x^2+2xy+3y^2=12\) with respect to \(x\). This gives \(2x+2(xy'+y)+6yy'=0\). Collecting \(y'\) terms gives \((2x+6y)y'=-(2x+2y)\), so \(y'=-(2x+2y)/(2x+6y)\). At \((0,2)\), the slope is \(-4/12=-1/3\).
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For the curve \(x^2+2xy+3y^2=12\), find \(dy/dx\) and evaluate the slope at \((0,2)\).

parts.answer: From first principles, \(q'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{q(x+h)-q(x)}{h}\). For \(q(x)=1/(x+2)\), the difference quotient is \(\frac{1}{h}\left(\frac{1}{x+h+2}-\frac{1}{x+2}\right)\). Combining fractions gives \(\frac{1}{h}\cdot\frac{(x+2)-(x+h+2)}{(x+h+2)(x+2)}=\frac{-1}{(x+h+2)(x+2)}\). Taking \(h\to0\) gives \(q'(x)=-1/(x+2)^2\), for \(x\ne-2\).
parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Using first principles, find the derivative of \(q(x)=\frac{1}{x+2}\), where \(x\ne-2\).

questions.stem: This question uses substitution, integration by parts, and rational integration.
questions.title: Integration methods

parts.answer: Let \(u=1+x^2\), so \(du=2x\,dx\). The bounds become \(u=1\) when \(x=0\), and \(u=2\) when \(x=1\). Hence \(\int_0^1 x\sqrt{1+x^2}\,dx=\frac12\int_1^2 u^{1/2}\,du=\frac12\left[\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_1^2=\frac13(2\sqrt2-1)\).
parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Evaluate \(\displaystyle \int_0^1 x\sqrt{1+x^2}\,dx\).

parts.answer: Use integration by parts with \(u=\ln x\) and \(dv=x^2\,dx\). Then \(du=dx/x\) and \(v=x^3/3\). Thus \(\int_0^1 x^2\ln x\,dx=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\ln x\right]_0^1-\frac13\int_0^1x^2\,dx\). The boundary term is \(0\), because \(x^3\ln x\to0\) as \(x\to0^+\). Therefore the integral is \(-\frac13\cdot\frac13=-\frac19\).
parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Evaluate \(\displaystyle \int_0^1 x^2\ln x\,dx\).

parts.answer: Divide first: \(\frac{4x^2+3x+5}{x^2+1}=4+\frac{3x+1}{x^2+1}\). Hence \(\int\frac{4x^2+3x+5}{x^2+1}\,dx=\int4\,dx+3\int\frac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx+\int\frac{dx}{x^2+1}\). These terms give \(4x+\frac32\ln(x^2+1)+\tan^{-1}x+C\).
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Evaluate \(\displaystyle \int\frac{4x^2+3x+5}{x^2+1}\,dx\).

questions.stem: Use principal arguments in \((-\pi,\pi]\) unless all arguments are requested.
questions.title: Complex form, roots, and exponential equations

parts.answer: The modulus is \(|z|=\sqrt{(-3)^2+(3\sqrt3)^2}=\sqrt{9+27}=6\). The point is in the second quadrant and has reference angle \(\pi/3\), so \(\operatorname{Arg}(z)=2\pi/3\). Therefore \(z=6e^{2\pi i/3}\).
parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write \(z=-3+3\sqrt3\,i\) in exponential form.

parts.answer: Write the right-hand side as \(27e^{-i\pi/2}\). The cube roots have modulus \(27^{1/3}=3\) and arguments \((-\pi/2+2k\pi)/3=-\pi/6+2k\pi/3\), for \(k=0,1,2\). Thus the roots are \(3e^{-i\pi/6}\), \(3e^{i\pi/2}\), and \(3e^{i7\pi/6}\). In rectangular form these are \(\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}-\frac32 i\), \(3i\), and \(-\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}-\frac32 i\).
parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Solve \(w^3=-27i\), giving all roots in exponential and rectangular form.

parts.answer: By De Moivre's theorem, \((\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^3=\cos3\theta+i\sin3\theta\). Expanding the left side gives real part \(\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta\). Equating real parts, \(\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta\). Since \(\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta\), this becomes \(\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta(1-\cos^2\theta)=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\).
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Use De Moivre's theorem to express \(\cos3\theta\) as a polynomial in \(\cos\theta\).

parts.answer: Let \(z=x+iy\). The equation is \(e^x e^{iy}=-2i=2e^{i(-\pi/2+2k\pi)}\). Matching moduli gives \(e^x=2\), so \(x=\ln2\). Matching arguments gives \(y=-\pi/2+2k\pi\). Hence \(z=\ln2+i(-\pi/2+2k\pi)\), where \(k\in\mathbb Z\).
parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Find all complex solutions of \(e^z=-2i\).

questions.stem: This question concerns positive-series tests, alternating series, and power-series endpoints.
questions.title: Series convergence and endpoint tests

parts.answer: Use limit comparison with \(b_n=1/n^2\). Then \(\frac{(4n^2+1)/(n^4+3)}{1/n^2}=\frac{n^2(4n^2+1)}{n^4+3}\to4\). This limit is positive and finite, and \(\sum1/n^2\) converges. Therefore the given series converges.
parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Use limit comparison to determine whether \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{4n^2+1}{n^4+3}\) converges.

parts.answer: Let \(a_n=n^3/3^n\). The ratio is \(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\frac{(n+1)^3}{3^{n+1}}\frac{3^n}{n^3}=\frac13(1+1/n)^3\). The limit is \(1/3\), which is less than \(1\). By the ratio test, the series converges.
parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Use the ratio test to determine whether \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^3}{3^n}\) converges.

parts.answer: The magnitudes are \(b_n=n/(n^2+1)\), and \(b_n\to0\). For large \(n\), \(b_n\) decreases because the denominator grows quadratically while the numerator grows linearly. The alternating series test gives convergence. For absolute convergence, compare \(n/(n^2+1)\) with \(1/n\): \(\frac{n/(n^2+1)}{1/n}=\frac{n^2}{n^2+1}\to1\). Since \(\sum1/n\) diverges, the absolute-value series diverges. The original series is conditionally convergent.
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Determine whether \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n+1}\frac{n}{n^2+1}\) is absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent.

parts.answer: Use the ratio test on absolute values. The ratio limit is \(|x+2|/5\), so the series converges absolutely when \(|x+2|<5\), giving \(-7<x<3\). At \(x=3\), the series is \(\sum1/n\), which diverges. At \(x=-7\), the series is \(\sum(-1)^n/n\), which converges by the alternating series test. The interval is \([-7,3)\).
parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Find the interval of convergence of \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(x+2)^n}{n5^n}\).

questions.section: Section E: Vector Spaces and Subspaces
questions.stem: This question concerns closure properties, subspaces of \(\mathbb R^3\), affine solution sets, and bases.
questions.title: Subspaces and affine planes

parts.answer: A non-empty subset \(W\) must be closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication using the operations from the parent vector space. Thus, if \(\mathbf u,\mathbf v\in W\), then \(\mathbf u+\mathbf v\in W\). If \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) and \(\mathbf u\in W\), then \(\lambda\mathbf u\in W\). Equivalently, every linear combination \(\lambda\mathbf u+\mu\mathbf v\) stays in \(W\).
parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the closure properties that a non-empty subset \(W\) of a vector space must satisfy to be a subspace.

parts.answer: The zero vector is in \(W\) because \(0-2\cdot0+0=0\). Let \(\mathbf u=(x_1,y_1,z_1)\) and \(\mathbf v=(x_2,y_2,z_2)\) be in \(W\), so \(x_1-2y_1+z_1=0\) and \(x_2-2y_2+z_2=0\). Then \((x_1+x_2)-2(y_1+y_2)+(z_1+z_2)=(x_1-2y_1+z_1)+(x_2-2y_2+z_2)=0\), so \(\mathbf u+\mathbf v\in W\). For \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), \(\lambda x_1-2\lambda y_1+\lambda z_1=\lambda(x_1-2y_1+z_1)=0\), so \(\lambda\mathbf u\in W\). Hence \(W\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb R^3\).
parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Prove that \(W=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:x-2y+z=0\}\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb R^3\).

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For \(A_c=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:x-2y+z=c\}\), classify for which real values of \(c\) the set \(A_c\) is a subspace, and explain your classification.

parts.answer: From the defining equation \(x-2y+z=0\), we have \(x=2y-z\). Let \(y=s\) and \(z=t\). Then \((x,y,z)=(2s-t,s,t)=s(2,1,0)+t(-1,0,1)\). The vectors \((2,1,0)\) and \((-1,0,1)\) are independent because \(a(2,1,0)+b(-1,0,1)=\mathbf0\) gives \(a=0\) from the second component and then \(b=0\) from the third component. A basis is \(\{(2,1,0),(-1,0,1)\}\), so \(\dim W=2\).
parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Find a basis and the dimension of \(W\).

questions.stem:
Consider the parameter-dependent system
\[
\begin{aligned}
x+y+z&=3,\\
2x+3y+z&=7,\\
x+2y+az&=b.
\end{aligned}
\]
questions.title: Classifying a parameter-dependent system

parts.answer: The coefficient matrix is \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\2&3&1\\1&2&a\end{pmatrix}\). Its determinant is \(1(3a-2)-1(2a-1)+1(4-3)=a\). Therefore the system has a unique solution exactly when \(a\ne0\).
parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the values of \(a\) for which the system has a unique solution.

parts.answer: Use row reduction on the augmented matrix. Apply \(R_2\leftarrow R_2-2R_1\) and \(R_3\leftarrow R_3-R_1\), giving rows \((0,1,-1|1)\) and \((0,1,a-1|b-3)\). Then \(R_3\leftarrow R_3-R_2\) gives \((0,0,a|b-4)\). When \(a=0\), this row is \((0,0,0|b-4)\). If \(b\ne4\), the system is inconsistent. If \(b=4\), the row is \(0=0\), leaving a free variable and infinitely many solutions.
parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Classify the non-unique cases as no solution or infinitely many solutions.

parts.answer: For \(a=0\) and \(b=4\), the reduced equations are \(x+y+z=3\) and \(y-z=1\). Let \(z=t\). Then \(y=1+t\), and \(x=3-y-z=3-(1+t)-t=2-2t\). Therefore the solutions are \((x,y,z)=(2-2t,1+t,t)\), where \(t\in\mathbb R\).
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For the infinitely many solution case, write the solution set in parameter form.

parts.answer: For \(a=1\), \(b=5\), the final reduced row gives \(z=1\). The row \(y-z=1\) gives \(y=2\). The first equation gives \(x+2+1=3\), so \(x=0\). The solution is \((x,y,z)=(0,2,1)\).
parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Solve the system for \(a=1\) and \(b=5\).

questions.section: Section G: Eigenvalues and Matrix Structure
questions.title: Eigenvectors, diagonalisation, and powers

parts.answer: Compute \(A(1,1,0)^T=(4,4,0)^T=4(1,1,0)^T\), so the eigenvalue is \(4\). Next, \(A(1,-1,0)^T=(2,-2,0)^T=2(1,-1,0)^T\), so the eigenvalue is \(2\). Finally, \(A(0,0,1)^T=(0,0,5)^T=5(0,0,1)^T\), so the eigenvalue is \(5\).
parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Verify that \(\mathbf v_1=(1,1,0)^T\), \(\mathbf v_2=(1,-1,0)^T\), and \(\mathbf v_3=(0,0,1)^T\) are eigenvectors of \(A\), and state the corresponding eigenvalues.

parts.answer: Use the eigenvectors as columns: \(P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&-1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\). The matching diagonal matrix is \(D=\begin{pmatrix}4&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&5\end{pmatrix}\). Since \(\det P=-2\ne0\), \(P\) is invertible, so \(A=PDP^{-1}\).
parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Construct matrices \(P\) and \(D\) such that \(A=PDP^{-1}\), and justify that this is a valid diagonalisation.

parts.answer: From \(A=PDP^{-1}\), \(A^n=PD^nP^{-1}\). Here \(D^n=\operatorname{diag}(4^n,2^n,5^n)\). Multiplying the \(2\times2\) block gives \(A^n=\begin{pmatrix}(4^n+2^n)/2&(4^n-2^n)/2&0\\(4^n-2^n)/2&(4^n+2^n)/2&0\\0&0&5^n\end{pmatrix}\).
parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Use the diagonalisation to find a formula for \(A^n\), where \(n\) is a positive integer.

parts.answer: The statement is true. If \(A=PDP^{-1}\) and \(A\) is invertible, then none of the diagonal entries of \(D\) is zero. Hence \(D^{-1}\) exists, and \(A^{-1}=PD^{-1}P^{-1}\). Since \(D^{-1}\) is diagonal, this is a diagonalisation of \(A^{-1}\).
parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Decide whether the statement is true or false, with justification: if \(A\) is invertible and diagonalizable, then \(A^{-1}\) is diagonalizable.
